_note: The cafe's small recurring universe. A low-probability prompt hook (see prompt.py) offers ONE of these per gen as an optional background easter egg — a name in a list, a line of fine print, a credit. Never the subject, never explained. Regulars notice; nobody else needs to. Add entries when a gen or a cat invents something worth keeping; keep hints short and usable in any era.

elements.name: Pepper
elements.hint: a shy cat, missing since roughly 1998, last seen behind the bus stop on 4th; answers to nothing; sightings are occasionally reported and never confirmed

elements.name: Eugene
elements.hint: a small spider who lives in a lobby corner; named by someone who had no authority to name him; unbothered; welcome

elements.name: Roy
elements.hint: a late husband, fondly remembered; had exactly one hobby at a time (woodworking, jam, model trains, birdhouses); believed simpler is best; understood a load-bearing seam

elements.name: Margot, age 4 ½
elements.hint: a child artist of local renown; signs everything with her age; her work has a sun in the corner; ask about Margot

elements.name: Frederick
elements.hint: somebody's cousin; claims to have been an extra in something; claims to detect flavors that are not there; claims a lot of things; sticks by every claim

elements.name: Mortimer
elements.hint: a kitten who dropped by once and is still talked about; whereabouts unknown; left an impression

elements.name: Deli Mustard
elements.hint: a band of unverifiable genre; plays $3 shows; no cover for birthdays; sometimes billed with Half Karen and the Eugene Eugenes

elements.name: The Good Wok
elements.hint: a takeout place; delivery 11–9, cash or check; menu item C4 is ??? and costs $0.00; the almond cookies come six to a bag

elements.name: 429 Persimmon Ln
elements.hint: an address where everything is perpetually for sale — the chairs, the photos, the lamps, a kettle; please don't haggle on the kettle

elements.name: the sign above the door
elements.hint: reads 'if the door is open, you are welcome inside.' — est. ~1962; quoted occasionally, attributed inconsistently

elements.name: the 3:47 light
elements.hint: every day at 3:47 the light hits the second shelf exactly right; some schedules, timetables, and instructions quietly account for this

elements.name: 555-PEPR
elements.hint: a phone number on tear-away tabs; calling it is never described; the tabs are always mostly taken

elements.name: Tindall's Confectionery
elements.hint: A neighborhood sweets counter that's 'had a counter here a long while'; hand-writes honest notes on every chocolate. Drop in anywhere as the old candy shop everyone's grandmother swore by.

elements.name: Slade Shallows
elements.hint: A shallow river ford where the water's low enough to wade or pole across; the kind of crossing named on old maps, flyers, and directions given by memory.

elements.name: Wren & Halloway
elements.hint: Wren & Halloway, Instrument Makers — a maker's mark (est. 1879) that can be stamped or engraved on any well-built object, from a harmonograph to a barometer.

elements.name: Ray Pruett
elements.hint: The neighbor on Linden who'll come stand in your yard and tell you what bird you keep hearing, by ear, for free — you never have to see it, and neither does he.

elements.name: Skipper the Seal
elements.hint: A cheerful cartoon mascot seal from an old draw-this talent ad, the kind of drugstore-rack character that could grin from any flyer, matchbook, or napkin in any era.

elements.name: Little Aumbry
elements.hint: A small out-of-the-way parish village, the kind with one old church and a rose window; good for a return address, a bus stop, or where someone's aunt retired.

elements.name: Small Weather, Passing
elements.hint: A gentle old tune called 'Small Weather, Passing' — the kind of half-remembered melody that turns up in a music box, on a jukebox, or hummed absently by someone at a sink.

elements.name: Old Haymaker's Switchel
elements.hint: A fizzy ginger-molasses-and-cider tonic pop bottled by Hollis & Son, prized on hot dusty afternoons; 2¢ back on the empty.

elements.name: Castellane's
elements.hint: The grand old downtown department store, famous for the roof aviary worth the whole elevator ride — droppable in any era as a passing shopping-trip mention.

elements.name: Prof. Orville Plumb
elements.hint: A long-ago mail-order huckster whose ten-dime ventriloquism course still turns up in classifieds and attic trunks; nobody ever quite mastered lesson three.

elements.name: Prewitt & Daughter
elements.hint: A hand-run dahlia-tuber farm out past the county fairgrounds — Ada Prewitt sells, daughter Ruth does the digging; a mail-order name to drop in any era.

elements.name: the Deaver boys
elements.hint: the local pack of rowdy brothers everyone knows by name — the ones who break the rule you just posted; usable in any era as background mischief.

elements.name: Ledbetter's Practical Kite-Craft
elements.hint: A well-thumbed how-to book on kite-making, forever in a revised printing with the figures slightly wrong; drops onto any shelf, table, or reading list in any era.

elements.name: Bett's Orchard
elements.hint: A roadside cider-press stand (est. 1971) where you fill your own jug by the quart; the wasps, Bett notes, are non-paying customers.

elements.name: Fenner's Mill
elements.hint: A wind-driven grist mill where old Ossie Fenner grinds any hour — the sails never stop turning, so you can come by whenever.

elements.name: Chef Pinder
elements.hint: A homey fictional frozen TV-dinner brand ('Chef Pinder's Own'), forever promising a whole hot supper in 25 minutes; drop it into any pantry, ad, or memory.

elements.name: Sunn's Prehistoric Gardens
elements.hint: A family-built roadside dinosaur park off the highway — nine hand-painted fiberglass giants you're allowed to touch, and a cherry slush at the window.

elements.name: Wilf
elements.hint: The fellow who keeps his own rival tally column chalked up beside the official one; nobody disputes his numbers, only his handwriting, which is a disgrace.

elements.name: A. Vasconcelos
elements.hint: The initialed name found stamped or inked on well-made small things — gauges, handles, tags — always with a date and never a first name, only ever the person who made it.

elements.name: Bev Hallonquist
elements.hint: The woman who can fix the thing everyone else has given up on, usually found with both arms inside it; keeps every shop order she's ever written, and knows exactly which drawer.

elements.name: Bickel & Sons Marking Device Works
elements.hint: A long-lived rubber-stamp and brass-die shop; its tiny maker's mark turns up on the handle of any stamp, and its impressions are always slightly crooked.

elements.name: Ferd
elements.hint: The maintenance man nobody ever sees; whatever's broken, worn, or leaking, Ferd says he'll get to it Monday. He has said this for some time.

elements.name: Wickwire's
elements.hint: A four-square downtown department store — six floors, tea room on the top — whose elevator indicator always reads a beat behind the car; turns up on bags, boxes, and charge accounts.

elements.name: Col
elements.hint: The person who taught you the trade, never present but constantly quoted — "Col says I talk" — always right, always mildly disapproving, and nobody ever explains who Col is.

elements.name: Kestrel & Fell
elements.hint: A street corner known for a small tin of yellow chalk screwed to the brick — always full, never once stolen, and nobody keeps track of who marks it.

elements.name: Mrs Kellsall
elements.hint: The neighbour two doors up; owns a striking clock that has never once kept time, and asks favours at teatime so you say yes before you've thought about it.

elements.name: R. Ramanujam
elements.hint: A clerk who keeps every ledger, list, and label in pencil because the roof has always leaked directly over his desk; two corrections circled, both to be believed.

elements.name: Frankenberry-Teague Stage Weather Co.
elements.hint: Kansas supplier of theatrical snow, rain, wind and fog, sold by the pound; their stenciled crates and stubborn price lists turn up in any basement, era, or back room.

retired.name: Hempstead Brothers Shows
retired.hint: A small traveling carnival out of Frankfort, Indiana, est. 1903 — three wagons grown old; the kind of outfit that rolls into any town's fairgrounds for a week and is gone.

retired.name: the Ferncliff gravel pit
retired.hint: An abandoned gravel pit behind the old cement works — a half-flooded local hangout where kids skip stones and nothing official ever happens.

retired.name: St. Aidwin's
retired.hint: The parish of a fictional English saint — turns up as a church, a school, a jumble sale or a bell tower; something's always going on down at St. Aidwin's.
